procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a Magistrate Court since the initial complaints were filed under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. and a Sessions Judge's order was reviewed by the High Court.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay at Aurangabad dated 23.10.2023 in CRLWP No.474 of 2023. This order approved the order of the Sessions Judge and issued further directions regarding investigation.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The 13 accused challenged the order of the Revisional Court (dated 23.03.2023) before the High Court through separate petitions titled under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and Article 227 of the Constitution of India. The High Court approved the Sessions Judge's order and issued further directions regarding investigation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via six Special Leave Petitions (SLPs). SLP (Crl.) No. 15433 of 2023 and SLP (Crl.) No. 15294 of 2023 were filed by the brother of the deceased. SLP (Crl.) Nos. 14734-14735 of 2023 were filed by the five purchasers. SLP (Crl.) No. 14585 of 2023 and SLP (Crl.) No. 14572 of 2023 were filed by the six police personnel. All SLPs were disposed of, with some being allowed subject to conditions.

issue.issue_text: Whether criminal proceedings arising from complaints under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, should be quashed based on a settlement between the parties where the complainants have been compensated for their losses.

facts: During the pendency of the case, a settlement was reached between the complainants (two tenants) and the 13 accused.
As part of the settlement, the subsequent purchasers of the property paid Rs. 10 lakhs to each of the tenants as compensation for their losses.
In return, the tenants filed affidavits with the court stating that they no longer wished to prosecute their criminal complaints.
application: The Supreme Court took note of the settlement and the affidavits filed by the tenants.

The Court reasoned that since the tenants' losses had been compensated and they themselves had expressed a desire to withdraw the complaint, continuing with the criminal proceedings would be pointless.
It concluded that any further investigation or trial in this matter would be an "exercise in futility" because the core dispute between the private parties had been resolved.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the settlement and decided to quash the criminal proceedings arising from the complaints under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., finding that the continuation of the case would serve no purpose after the complainants were compensated and had agreed to drop the matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether criminal proceedings arising from complaints under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, should be quashed based on a settlement between the parties where the complainants have been compensated for their losses.
appellant_arguments: The petitioners (the accused parties) argued that a settlement had been reached between them and the complainants (tenants).
Based on this settlement, where the complainants were compensated, they prayed for the criminal proceedings arising from the complaints under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. to be quashed.
respondent_arguments: The respondents (complainants/tenants) supported the quashing of the proceedings.
They filed affidavits confirming they had been compensated (paid Rs. 10 lacs each) and stated that they did not wish to further prosecute their complaints.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No binding legal rule was established as the case was disposed of based on a settlement between the parties, which included quashing criminal proceedings initiated under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: Directions for police personnel to pay compensation to tenants should not be treated as adverse to their interests in matters of promotion, nor should the order be kept in their service records.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the criminal proceedings should be quashed because the complainants had settled the matter with the accused, received financial compensation for their losses, and had formally stated their desire to withdraw the complaint. Consequently, any further legal proceedings would serve no purpose.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a pragmatic test based on the futility of continuing criminal proceedings when the underlying dispute has been resolved between the parties and the victim no longer wishes to prosecute.
why_respondent_won: The complainants (respondents) supported the quashing of proceedings, filing affidavits confirming they had been compensated with Rs. 10 lacs each and stating they did not wish to further prosecute their complaints.
The court found that since the complainants' losses had been compensated, the primary grievance was resolved, making further proceedings unnecessary.
policy_considerations: The court determined that continuing the investigation or trial after the complainants had been compensated and had withdrawn their support for the prosecution would be an 'exercise in futility,' reflecting a policy against the wasteful expenditure of judicial and state resources.
